findings.claim: The canonical-output limit lacks the required exact-boundary test. The existing test cannot distinguish the implemented inclusive limit from an incorrect exclusive limit.
findings.evidence: test_canonical_expansion_guard verifies a canonical serialization larger than 262144 bytes and another strictly smaller than 262144 bytes. It never supplies an otherwise accepted contract whose canonical serialization is exactly 262144 bytes. Changing the production predicate from `len(canonical) > 262144` to `len(canonical) >= 262144` would therefore leave these assertions satisfied. Acceptance criteria 5 and 7 require inclusive admission and predicate-specific at/over-limit coverage for every resource boundary.
findings.requestedFix: Add independently constructed, schema-valid canonical-output vectors of exactly 262144 and 262145 bytes. Establish their canonical lengths using the accepted serializer, keep input size and all other resource limits within bounds, assert exact canonical-byte preservation for the at-limit vector, and assert resource_limit for the one-byte-over vector.

findings.claim: The contract-subclass rejection predicate is not independently tested: the only StrCanary invocation is short-circuited by the payload-subclass rejection.
findings.evidence: test_types_and_precedence passes BytesCanary and StrCanary together. In _map, `type(payload) is not bytes or type(contract) is not str` rejects the payload before evaluating the contract predicate. Removing the contract exact-type check would therefore leave this test green, while an exact bytes payload paired with StrCanary could invoke its supplied comparison method during supported-contract checking. The production predicate is correct as supplied, but the required security-boundary regression coverage is missing.
findings.requestedFix: Add an independent public-boundary test using an exact built-in bytes payload and StrCanary as the contract, asserting sanitized invalid_input without invoking subclass methods. Also exercise BytesCanary with an exact built-in supported contract so each exact-type predicate has its own canary case.
